landmarks.name: Lake Malawi
landmarks.writeup: One of the largest lakes in Africa, known for its clear waters and diverse fish species.

wiki.extract: Malawi has a developing economy. It generates $7.522 billion by gross domestic product as of 2019, and is predominantly agricultural, with about 80% of the population living in rural areas. The landlocked country in south central Africa ranks among the world's poorest and least developed countries. Approximately 50% of the population lives below the national poverty line, with 25% living in extreme poverty.

landmarks.name: Liwonde National Park
landmarks.writeup: A prominent wildlife reserve home to elephants, hippos, and various bird species.

wiki.extract: Liwonde National Park, also known as Liwonde Wildlife Reserve, is a national park in southern Malawi, near the Mozambique border. The park was established in 1973, and has been managed by the nonprofit conservation organization African Parks since August 2015. African Parks built an electric fence around the perimeter of the park to help mitigate human-wildlife conflict. In early 2018, the adjacent Mangochi Forest Reserve was also brought under African Parks' management, almost doubling the size of the protected area.

landmarks.name: Mount Mulanje
landmarks.writeup: The highest peak in Malawi, popular for hiking and its unique biodiversity.

wiki.extract: The Mulanje Massif, also known as Mount Mulanje, is a large inselberg and World Heritage Site in southern Malawi. Sapitwa Peak, the highest point on the massif at 3,002 m, is the highest point in Malawi. It lies 65 km east of Blantyre, rising sharply from the surrounding plains of Phalombe and the Mulanje district. It forms part of a proposed ecoregion, to be called the South East Africa Montane Archipelago (SEAMA).

cultural_events.name: Lake of Stars Festival
cultural_events.writeup: An annual music and arts festival held on the shores of Lake Malawi, attracting international artists.

wiki.extract: Lake of Stars Festival is an annual three-day international festival held on the shores of Lake Malawi, the third largest lake in Africa. The first festival took place in 2004 and attracts over 4,000 attendees with musical acts mainly from Africa and Europe.

cultural_events.name: Gule Wamkulu
cultural_events.writeup: A traditional dance of the Chewa people, performed during important ceremonies and festivals.

wiki.extract: Gule Wamkulu is a ritual masquerade and dance tradition of the Chewa people in Malawi, Zambia, and Mozambique. It is performed by initiated members of the Nyau society. The name is widely translated as "the great dance".

food_writeup: Malawian cuisine features staple foods like nsima (a maize porridge), often served with vegetables, beans, or fish from Lake Malawi.
brief_history: Malawi gained independence from British colonial rule in 1964. It was formerly known as Nyasaland and has since developed as a multi-party democracy.

important_people.name: Joyce Banda
important_people.description: Former President and first female head of state

current_conflicts: Malawi is generally peaceful but faces challenges related to poverty, governance, and occasional political tensions.

commentary.inflation_management: Malawi's inflation history is one of repeated devaluation-driven spirals. It was contained at 7-9% from 2007 to 2011, then the 2012 kwacha devaluation (under Joyce Banda) sent it to 21.3% in 2012 and 28.3% in 2013. Tighter policy brought it back to single digits by 2018-2021, but forex shortages, Cyclone Freddy, and drought reignited it: 20.8% in 2022, 28.8% in 2023, and a series high of 32.2% in 2024, with 28.4% projected for 2025. The Reserve Bank of Malawi has hiked rates aggressively, but with chronic forex scarcity and a managed exchange rate under constant pressure, monetary policy fights pass-through it cannot prevent.
commentary.debt_management: Malawi's debt went from relief to crisis in under two decades. HIPC completion in 2006 brought it to 17.9% of GDP, the series low. Then came Cashgate-era borrowing, kwacha devaluations that inflated the local-currency value of external debt, and repeated climate and COVID shocks: the ratio climbed relentlessly to 87.6% in 2024, the series high, easing to a projected 77.8% in 2025. Malawi is now in debt distress, with domestic debt (expensive Treasury bills) the acute pressure point. Restructuring discussions have dragged on, and debt service crowds out everything else in the budget.

key_events.event: HIPC completion-point relief cut debt to 17.9% of GDP.
President Bingu wa Mutharika died in office; Joyce Banda devalued the kwacha; inflation surged past 20%.
'Cashgate' corruption scandal saw donors withdraw budget support.
2019 election annulled by the courts; Lazarus Chakwera won the 2020 rerun.
Cyclone Freddy (2023) and drought devastated agriculture; inflation hit 28.8%.
September 16, 2025: Peter Mutharika (85) defeated Chakwera with 56.8% of the vote, returning to power on the economic crisis.

commentary.outlook_next_decade: The base case is continued distress management: debt near 78% of GDP, inflation near 30%, and growth hostage to rains and forex. Upside depends on a credible debt restructuring and the new Mutharika government's stabilization plan; downside is a disorderly currency collapse. Uncertainty is high: Malawi has the policies of a crisis country but not yet the resolution of one, and the 2025 political reset is untested.
commentary.caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
